lesson.menu_title: Who Does What -- Controls and Owners
lesson.menu_desc: The committee approved the deal, with one condition: a one-page map that names every control and the person behind it. Today you learn to put a whole sentence inside a noun -- the person who signs off, the control that catches a breach, the alert which fires by itself -- 34 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 17 -- Who Does What: Controls and Owners
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Sergio Takashi Tanaka | Lesson 17 -- Who Does What: Controls and Owners

listenings.text: Sergio, it is Marina. Before you send that page tonight, three things, and they are the three the committee actually reads. First, remember what a control map is for. It is not a description of the process. Nobody in that room wants to know how the check works. They want to see that somebody answers for every line, so put a name against every control and do not hide behind a department. Second, mark the manual ones. Two of ours are manual, the daily exposure check and the quarterly file review, and that matters because a manual control depends on a person being at a desk that morning. A system does not go on holiday, and a person does. If you do not mark them, the first auditor who reads the page will mark them for you, and it will look like we did not know. Third, and this is the one people forget. A control with no named deputy is not a control yet. It stops the day the owner is away, and a control that stops is a gap with a nice title. So name a deputy on every line, including mine. Send it before midnight.

Sergio, Paulo here, from the credit desk. Two minutes on the lines, because the auditors arrive next month and they always start in the same place. The first line is us. It is the team that takes the risk and runs the control, day after day, and it reports to the business. The second line is the team that checks the first line, and the whole point of it is that it does not report to us. If it did, it would be checking its own work, and that is not a check at all. Now, the question. Every auditor I have ever met asks one question, in different words, all day long. Who is accountable. Not who did it, not who has the password, not which system it sits in. Who answers for it when it goes wrong. Have that name ready for every line, and say it without looking at the page. And one mistake to avoid when you write the map, because I see it every quarter. Do not write a team name where a person should be. Risk Systems is fine for an automated alert, but a team cannot answer a question in a meeting, and a team cannot be on the phone at eight in the morning. A person can. Good luck.

extra_audio.text: First, start with the control itself, and say in one line what it catches. Then name the person who owns it, never a team. Next, name the deputy who covers that person when they are away. After that, say how often it runs, and whether it is manual or automatic. Finally, finish with the bottleneck: the one step that only one person can give.
